entities.name: Royal Opera House
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Royal Opera House at Covent Garden in London is the United Kingdom's principal opera and ballet venue, home to the Royal Opera and the Royal Ballet, dating from 1732 with the current building opened in 1858. The Royal Ballet Company, founded by Ninette de Valois in 1931, developed its own British classical ballet tradition distinct from Russian models — and trained Margot Fonteyn, whose 1962 partnership with Rudolf Nureyev became the most celebrated in ballet history.

The current building, designed by Edward Barry, has been the scene of premieres of major works by Britten, Walton, and Tippett, and the debut venue for many of the 20th century's greatest singers. The ROH underwent a complete reconstruction 1997-1999, creating a new backstage, a second stage, and public spaces while preserving the Victorian auditorium. The £78 million project was the largest arts capital project in UK history.

The Royal Ballet's Margot Fonteyn-Rudolf Nureyev partnership (1962-1979) transcended ballet: Nureyev's defection from the Soviet Union had made him a Cold War symbol, and his partnership with Fonteyn — she 43, he 24, when they first danced together — was a sensation that packed every house and brought ballet to television audiences across Britain. Their 1962 Giselle at Covent Garden received 89 curtain calls. The ROH also hosts the BBC Proms final night traditions and serves as a cornerstone of British cultural identity.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Royal Opera House created British classical ballet through Ninette de Valois's institution-building, and the Fonteyn-Nureyev partnership's 89-curtain-call Giselle represents the most celebrated moment in 20th-century ballet history.
